content.intro: Learn content security policy through a compact visual, an inspectable Django example, and a practical verification task.
content.why_it_matters: Content Security Policy matters because a Django project has to behave predictably across requests, database state, configuration, and deployments. Understanding this piece makes the surrounding application easier to test, maintain, and secure.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: This lesson examines content security policy as part of security and privacy. The objective is to understand the behavior, connect it to the listed subtopics, and verify it with a small example rather than relying on memorized syntax.

content_blocks.title: What to cover
content_blocks.text: The source syllabus for this lesson names: CSP directives and source policies; Enforcing versus report-only policies; Script nonces; Protecting against content injection; Django's built-in CSP support, introduced in Django 6.0. Keep these distinct concepts together: know what each item does, when it applies, and what assumption must be verified in your project.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Content Security Policy
content_blocks.code: Trust boundary: browser/user input → validate/authorize on server → parameterized ORM/SQL → escaped response → security tests
content_blocks.expected_output: The trust boundary shows that untrusted input must be checked before use and output must be appropriate to the target context.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Common pitfalls include skipping a required configuration/import, copying a fragment without its model or URL context, trusting client input, or treating a development-only behavior as production-ready. Check the earliest failing assumption, consult the version-specific docs, and add a regression test for the failure you found.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a framework fragment without its imports, configuration, model, or URL context.
common_mistakes.why: The snippet may be incomplete when separated from a Django project.
common_mistakes.fix: Use the stated prerequisites and run the relevant management check or focused test.

common_mistakes.problem: Trusting input or relying only on a happy-path example.
common_mistakes.why: Invalid values, unauthorized requests, or concurrent activity can violate assumptions.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate on the server and add a negative or boundary test.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating the development sample as production-ready.
common_mistakes.why: Production hosting, secrets, storage, monitoring and resource limits differ from local use.
common_mistakes.fix: Follow the current deployment/security references and document untested areas.
